title: Model 1
html:
Background

This project aims to establish a cell–cell adhesion system using coiled-coil proteins. However, in the actual system, coiled-coils are placed in the periplasmic region via membrane proteins and linkers, which restricts their rotational freedom. Therefore, it is necessary to consider not only whether the coiled-coils themselves can form a stable complex, but also whether CoilE and CoilR can come close to interact effectively when tethered to the membrane.

To address this, the Dry Lab conducted a stepwise analysis using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to support the Wet Lab's design:

  1. Evaluate the binding stability of the coiled-coil complex.
  2. Estimate the distance range over which interactions between CoilE and CoilR can be maintained and establish a design criterion.
  3. Compare different linkers attached to the coiled-coils based on this criterion.

・Evaluation of the Thermodynamic and Structural Stability of the Coiled-Coil Complex

To evaluate the binding stability of the coiled-coil complex from a free-energy perspective, we performed pulling simulations and umbrella sampling to calculate the potential of mean force (PMF) through the following steps.

  1. Conventional MD simulation

Perform MD simulations (100 ns, 120 ns, etc.).

  1. Pulling simulation (Video 2)

Starting from the final structure obtained in Step 1, gradually changing the distance between CoilE and CoilR to generate initial configurations at different separation distances for umbrella sampling.

  1. Umbrella sampling (Video 3)

Perform MD simulations (5 ns) while restraining the coiled-coils at each separation distance.

  1. PMF (Potential of Mean Force) calculation

Calculate the PMF using the Weighted Histogram Analysis Method (WHAM).

In addition, we evaluated the structural stability of the coiled-coil complex. First, we performed a 100 ns MD simulation of the isolated coiled-coil complex (Video 1). During the simulation, neither significant dissociation of CoilE and CoilR nor unfolding of their α-helical structures was observed, suggesting that the coiled-coil complex can remain stable in its bound state.

We then quantitatively evaluated its structural stability using the following metrics:

  • RMSD (Root Mean Square Deviation)
  • SASA (Solvent Accessible Surface Area)
  • Center-of-mass distance
  • Rg (Radius of Gyration)
  • Number of hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, and hydrophobic interactions

Results The PMF analysis revealed that the PMF increased as the distance between CoilE and CoilR increased (Figure 1). This suggests that the bound state of CoilE and CoilR is thermodynamically more stable than the separated state.

                                                                 figure1. PMF of the coiled-coils

The results of the structural stability evaluation of the coiled-coil complex using each metric are presented below.

・RMSD

We compared the initial structure of the coiled-coil complex at 0 ns with its structure at each time point during the simulation. As shown in Figure 2 , the RMSD remained around 0.1 nm and stayed below 0.25 nm throughout the simulation. These results indicate that the coiled-coil complex did not undergo significant structural changes relative to its initial structure.

                                                                figure2. RMSD of the coiled-coils

・SASA The SASA remained nearly constant, with an average value of 66.9 nm², fluctuating approximately between 60 and 75 nm². The coefficient of variation (CV) was low (1.99%). These results suggest that no major structural changes occurred, such as significant unfolding of the coiled-coils that would increase their solvent-exposed surface area.

                                                                figure3. SASA of the coiled-coils

・Center-of-Mass Distance The center-of-mass distance between CoilE and CoilR remained within the range of 0.4–0.8 nm. The PMF analysis suggested that the interactions between CoilE and CoilR become sufficiently weak at a separation distance of approximately 2.5 nm. Throughout the simulation, the center-of-mass distance remained well below this value, indicating no tendency for the coiled-coil complex to dissociate.

                                              figure4. Center-of-Mass Distance of the coiled-coils

・Rg (Radius of Gyration) The radius of gyration (Rg) remained nearly constant, with an average value of approximately 1.86 nm and a low coefficient of variation (CV) of approximately 0.73%. These results indicate that the overall compactness of the coiled-coil complex remained largely unchanged, with no significant structural disruption.

                                                             figure5. Rg of the coiled-coils

・Number of Hydrogen Bonds, Salt Bridges, and Hydrophobic Interactions The number of hydrogen bonds ranged from 2 to 17, the number of salt bridges ranged from 1 to 10, and the number of residue pairs involved in hydrophobic interactions ranged from 18 to 31. These results confirmed that hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, and hydrophobic interactions were continuously maintained throughout the simulation.

                                    figure6. Number of Hydrogen Bonds between the coiled-coils

                                    figure7. Number of Salt Bridges between the coiled-coils

                           figure8. Number of Hydrophobic Interactions between the coiled-coils

All things considered, these results suggest that the coiled-coil complex maintained a stable bound state without significant structural disruption under the simulation conditions, while preserving its interfacial interactions. Both the structural stability analysis using conventional MD simulations and the free-energy analysis using PMF suggest that the coiled-coil complex has the potential to serve as an adhesion component in our system.

However, even if the coiled-coil complex itself exhibits stable binding, CoilE and CoilR are tethered to membrane proteins via linkers in the actual system, which restricts their mobility. Therefore, depending on the length and flexibility of the linkers, CoilE and CoilR may not be able to approach each other closely enough or form sufficient interactions.

As shown in Figure 1, the PMF began to plateau at a separation distance of approximately 2.3–2.5 nm between CoilE and CoilR, suggesting that the contribution of their interactions becomes small beyond this distance. Therefore, we used this distance range as one of the criteria for linker design and selected linkers to keep the separation distance between the coiled-coils below 2.3 nm.

・Linker Selection We constructed a model of our system incorporating the membrane environment and performed MD simulations to compare the binding states of the coiled-coil complex using four types of linkers proposed by the Wet Lab.

Results Differences in the binding states of the coiled-coil complex were observed depending on the linker used, and (GGGGS)3 was identified as a promising candidate. ・(GGGGS)n Linker In the system using the (GGGGS)3 linker, the coiled-coil complex maintained its bound state without significant dissociation throughout the 10 ns simulation. In addition, hydrogen bonds, salt bridges, and hydrophobic interactions were continuously maintained (see Figures 9, 10, and 11, and Table 1), with some interactions showing an increasing trend over time. ・(EAAAK)n Linker In the systems using the rigid (EAAAK)6 and (EAAAK)2 linkers, the linkers appeared to push against the coiled-coils, causing them to tilt. In addition, there were periods during which hydrophobic interactions were lost. ・GSSGSSGS Linker and (GS)n Linker In the systems using GSSGSSGS and (GS)4, which are flexible linkers with relatively high rigidity due to their higher serine content, interactions such as salt bridges were temporarily lost. The binding states of the coiled-coil complexes were less stable than those observed with the (GGGGS)3 linker.

In conclution, these results suggest that allowing CoilE and CoilR to approach each other while maintaining sufficient rotational freedom is important for forming stable interactions. In particular, the glycine-rich (GGGGS)3 linker appears to facilitate favorable positioning of CoilE and CoilR, making it the most promising linker candidate among those compared in this study.

Summary The results of the analyses described above were incorporated into the project in the following ways.

  1. Continued Use of Coiled-Coils as Adhesion Components Since the coiled-coil complex maintained a stable bound state throughout the 100 ns MD simulation, the Wet Lab can using coiled-coils as adhesion components in the system based on logical evidence.
  2. Establishment of a Design Criterion for the Distance Between Coiled-Coils The PMF analysis provided an estimate of the separation distance at which interactions between CoilE and CoilR become weak. By using this distance as a criterion for evaluating whether the coiled-coils could maintain stable interactions, we were able to select linkers in a more rational manner.
  3. Selection of the Linker on the Intimin Side MD simulations incorporating the membrane environment were performed to compare several linkers. Among the candidates tested, (GGGGS)3 was found to be the most effective at maintaining the bound state of the coiled-coil complex. Based on these results, which were shared with the Wet Lab, (GGGGS)3 was selected as the linker on the Intimin side. Overall, the modeling performed by the Dry Lab helped narrow down the candidates for experimental validation by the Wet Lab, thereby reducing the need for trial-and-error experimentation.
